interviewQuestions.question: Design the recommendation system for a video app's homepage.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd structure this as a funnel, since no single model scores every video for every user in real time. First, **candidate generation**: pull a few hundred plausible videos from multiple sources — a two-tower collaborative model, a content-based match on the user's recent watches, and a trending/popularity pool for cold-start coverage.

Second, **ranking**: score that shortlist with a richer model using dense features — watch-history embeddings, video metadata, time-of-day, device — trained to predict something closer to real value than a raw click, like predicted watch-time completion, since optimizing pure CTR breeds clickbait.

Third, **re-ranking / business rules**: de-duplicate near-identical videos, cap how many videos from one creator appear in a row, inject a small quota of exploratory/novel content, and apply any policy filters.

I'd close on evaluation: validate offline with NDCG and precision@k on held-out data as a cheap first filter, but only trust an A/B test measuring real watch-time and return-visit rate before shipping, since offline and online rankings often disagree.

**Testing:** whether you can structure an open-ended system design answer as a funnel with a labeling choice and an evaluation plan, not just name a model.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Video homepage recommender design

interviewQuestions.question: Why do most production learning-to-rank systems use a pointwise approach even though pairwise or listwise objectives more directly match the actual ranking goal?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The gap between what's theoretically ideal and what's practically deployed comes down to simplicity, calibration, and infrastructure fit, not a belief that pointwise is more accurate. A pointwise model predicts an independent score per item — often a real probability, like predicted click-through or watch-time completion — and then sorts by that score. This has two properties production systems care about a lot: the score is independently interpretable and calibratable (you can say "this item has a 12% predicted click probability" and check that against real observed rates, useful for other decisions like ad pricing or a business-rule threshold), and it slots cleanly into standard supervised learning infrastructure and loss functions everyone already knows how to train and debug.

Pairwise and listwise objectives directly optimize the thing you actually care about — getting relative order right, or optimizing a whole list's quality against a metric like NDCG — a more faithful match to the real goal. But they're harder to work with operationally: pairwise training needs constructing comparison pairs at scale, multiplying the effective training set size and adding real engineering complexity; listwise objectives require a differentiable approximation of a ranking metric, mathematically trickier and slower to train and iterate on than a simple pointwise loss. There's also a practical benefit pointwise scores get for free: an independent per-item score is separately reusable elsewhere in the product (a probability shown to a stakeholder, a threshold-based decision) in a way a purely relative pairwise or listwise score isn't.

So the trade a team makes by defaulting to pointwise: accept a slightly less-than-optimal match to the true ranking objective for a simpler, more calibratable, more reusable, easier-to-iterate-on system — usually worthwhile unless pairwise/listwise gains are large enough to justify the added complexity.

**Testing:** whether you can articulate the real engineering trade-off (calibration, complexity, reusability) rather than assuming pointwise is simply "good enough" without explaining why teams accept the theoretical gap.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why pointwise ranking dominates in practice

interviewQuestions.question: Your recommender's offline NDCG improved significantly with a new ranking model, but the A/B test showed no meaningful change in the real business metric. How do you reconcile that, and what would you check?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I wouldn't treat this as a contradiction that invalidates one measurement — offline and online metrics answer genuinely different questions, and disagreement between them is common enough to be an expected outcome to investigate, not a surprising failure. Offline NDCG measures how well the model ranks a fixed, historical, labeled dataset — a proxy for ranking quality computed against data reflecting past user behavior under the *old* model, with labels that themselves may be biased by what the old system happened to show (position bias in click-derived relevance labels being the classic culprit). The online A/B test measures actual behavior change in real users exposed to the new ranking live — a more direct signal, but also noisier and diluted by factors offline metrics don't see.

My investigation path: first, check whether the offline labels themselves might be stale or biased in a way that inflated the NDCG improvement without reflecting genuine relevance — if the held-out set was built from historical clicks under the old ranking, a model that ranks similarly to what historically got clicked can score well on NDCG without producing better *real* recommendations, since the label already encodes the old system's biases. Second, check whether the business metric is downstream or sensitive enough to detect what NDCG measured — a better top-10 ranking might move click-through rate but take longer to surface in a slower metric like retention, and the test's duration might not have been long enough to detect a real but small effect. Third, segment the A/B results — an aggregate "no change" can hide a real win for one segment offset by a neutral or negative effect elsewhere.

Whatever the finding, the lesson holds: offline metrics are a fast pre-ship filter to reject clearly worse models, never sufficient proof a change helps the business — exactly why the A/B test is the final gate.

**Testing:** whether you can reconcile a real offline/online disagreement methodically (label bias, metric sensitivity, segmentation) rather than dismissing either measurement.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Reconciling an offline win with a null online result
